en: The Proof of Exclusion (Apohasiddhi). Homage to the glorious Lokanātha.
The referent of a word is defined as *apoha*. Now, what is this so-called *apoha*?
Is it that which is excluded from others?

Alternatively, based on the etymological derivation that "either something else is excluded from this" or "something else is excluded in this," what is intended is either the external object itself as distinguished from those of a different class,
or the mental image (buddhyākāra).
Alternatively, there are three positions: that "apoha" means removal (*apohana*), that it means exclusion (*apoha*), or that it means mere differentiation (*anyavyāvṛttimātra*).
First of all, the first two positions are not tenable, because by the name "apoha," it is precisely a positive entity (*vidhi*) that is intended to be expressed.
Even the last [alternative] is untenable, because it is contradicted by actual cognition;
for, in the case of the verbal cognition "there is fire on the mountain," the cognition is observed to represent only a positive form,
not as merely manifesting a negation such as "it is not the case that there is no fire."
And it is well known that where something is sublated by perception, there is no room for other means of proof.
Now, even if there is no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in the form "I cognize a cessation," nevertheless,
the very mention of the object that has ceased is itself the mention of the cessation.
For there is no cognition of a qualified object that does not involve the cognition of its qualifier.

Therefore, just as for others, a conceptual cognition is a "cognition of a universal" because the common form flashes forth even in the absence of the explicit thought "I cognize a universal," so too, the cognition of exclusion (*nivṛttibuddhi*), projected by the notion of cessation, extends the conventional usage of the "cognition of apoha. If this is argued:
Now, if the establishment of the cognition of a universal is based on the manifestation of a common form as having a positive (vidhi) nature,

then what follows for the establishment of the cognition of exclusion (nivṛtti) when the mental state lacks the manifestation of a positive form? Therefore, even in the absence of a mental form such as "I cognize an exclusion," if there were a manifestation of the form of exclusion, [it would be established].
Who indeed would deny the existence of the cognition of exclusion (*nivṛtti*)?

Otherwise, if there were no appearance [of that exclusion], the linguistic usage based on its cognition could not occur; thus, even in a mind having the form of a cow, let it be considered a cognition of a horse.
Now, it might be argued that the cognition of exclusion is included as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Nevertheless, if the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) takes such a form as "that which is excluded from non-cows," then let there be an entry of that [exclusion] as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*);
however, the cognition is "cow.
And in that case, because the qualifier characterized by exclusion (*nivṛtti*), even though it exists, is not brought forward (*utkalita*) therein.
How is that established through cognition? Now, if this is the thought:
"That which manifests as a positive form (vidhirūpa) also possesses the exclusion of others (parāpoha); therefore, it is called the cognition of that [positive form]."
Nevertheless, even in the case of exclusion (*apoha*), it is the positive entity itself that appears directly as the mere relation.
Moreover, in this way, the fact that even perception has exclusion as its object becomes unavoidable—
especially for conceptual cognition, which, while delineating the exclusion of one thing, perceives everything else as excluded.

Therefore, since conceptual cognition, like perception, apprehends a positive form (*vidhyākāra*), its object is exclusively a positive entity and not the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*); how then can it be proclaimed that the meaning of a word is *apoha*?
To this, it is replied:
By the term "exclusion" (apoha), we do not intend a mere positive affirmation alone,
nor merely the exclusion of others; rather, the meaning of words is a positive affirmation qualified by the exclusion of others.

Consequently, there is no room for the faults that befall each of the individual positions. As for the view of the proponents of affirmation (*vidhivādins*), who hold that when a cow is perceived, its exclusion (*apoha*)—namely, that it is not of the nature of another—is subsequently determined through implication; or the view of the proponents of negation (*pratiṣedhavādins*), who hold that when the exclusion of others is perceived, the thing excluded from others is ascertained through implication.
That is not correct,
because even for the first [cognition], no sequence of apprehension is observed;
for no one, having apprehended the positive injunction (*vidhi*), subsequently understands the exclusion (*apoha*) through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*).

Alternatively, one may apprehend exclusion (*apoha*), thinking "this is excluded from others"; therefore, the cognition of a cow is called the "apprehension of what is excluded from others" (*anyāpoḍhapratipatti*).
Even though it was stated that there is no verbal mention of the term "excluded from others," [it is still so].
Nevertheless, it is not a case of non-comprehension at all,
because the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), which serves as the qualifier, has been applied to the word "cow" precisely in the sense of being excluded from non-cows.
Just as when the word *indīvara*— which is applied to a blue lotus— is understood as a blue lotus, the manifestation of its blueness at that very moment is unavoidable.

Likewise, when the word "cow" is applied to that which is excluded from non-cows (*agavāpoha*), the manifestation of the exclusion of non-cows (*ago'poha*) is unavoidable at the very same time as the cognition of the cow, because it functions as its qualifier.

Just as perception possesses the power to forcibly grasp the absence of form and thereby produce a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of that absence, so too the conceptual constructions of positive entities (*vidhivikalpa*) are said to "grasp the absence" precisely by their power to instigate an activity corresponding to that [positive object].

However, the apprehension of absence in the form of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*)— which is the awareness of a determinate intrinsic nature— is indistinguishable in both cases; otherwise, if the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) were not grasped at the time of understanding the meaning from a word,
how could there be activity by way of avoiding what is other?
Then, being urged with the command "Bind the cow," one might as well bind horses and other animals as well.
As for what Vācaspati said—
that individuals must be qualified by their genus— [that too is untenable].

It is the domain of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and words; and since the form of those individuals possessing that [universal] is excluded from what is not of that class, it is understood through implication (*arthataḥ*) as such. Therefore, when told "Bind the cow," one binds horses and the like [only by mistake].

This too is refuted by this very [argument]: for even if an additional universal (*jāti*) were introduced, if the form of the individuals is indeed excluded from what is not of that class, [then the same result follows].
In that case, since [particulars] become objects of both words and conceptual cognitions in that very form, how can there be an avoidance of non-exclusion from what is other than that?
Or, if the form of the individual is not excluded from what is of a different class,
and is not perceived as such, [then the objection remains].

Or, if it is argued that this is simply the clarity of the universal (*jāti*), how can its cognition occur even through the object? This has already been largely explained. Now, suppose it is excluded from others solely by the power of the universal;
let it be so excluded either by the power of the universal or by the power of its own causal series.

In either case, when there is a cognition of exclusion, there is indeed a cognition of that which is excluded. Furthermore, in the establishment of the linguistic convention for the word "cow" as the exclusion of non-cows (*ago'poha*), there is no fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*);
for such a fault would only have scope if the convention were established in relation to a universal (*sāmānya*) or its possessor (*tadvat*).
For "universal" (sāmānya) does not here refer to a mere universal in general, because that would entail the absurd consequence of applying the word "cow" even to a horse;
rather, it refers specifically to "cowness" (gotva).
And by that much, the same fault remains.
Because if the cow is not cognized, the universal "cowness" (gotva-sāmānya) is not cognized;
and if the universal "cowness" is not cognized, that which is denoted by the word "cow" is not cognized.
Therefore, that mental image (*vikalpabuddhyākāra*) which, based on the perception of a single individual, appears as if it were common to all individuals and exists externally—[is what is meant].
In that regard, when establishing the convention "this is a cow," there is no fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Furthermore, once the application of the word "cow" is intended, it is appropriate that the remainder [of things] is also denoted by the word "non-cow.

Nor is there any contradiction between the exclusion of others (*anyāpoḍha*) and the exclusion itself (*anyāpoha*), nor any impairment of the relationship between the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Because there is no mutual exclusion between them,
and because there exists a coreferential relationship (sāmānādhikaraṇya),
just like the absence of a jar on the ground.
For it is well known even among children that contradiction exists through intrinsic nature (*svābhāva*) and not through the absence of another (*parābhāva*).
In the expression "this path leads to Śrughna," exclusion (*apoha*) is indeed understood;
for, in relation to other paths not under discussion, it is understood as "this very one."
In relation to undesired locations that are the opposite of Śrughna, it is indeed Śrughna [that is understood].
Because there is no interruption, as in the case of a forest path, it simply presents itself.

Since exclusions are easily found at every step—such as the exclusion of a caravan, a messenger, and so forth—it follows that from a word whose nature is apoha, there is an understanding of a positive form (vidhirūpa).
Just as from the word "puṇḍarīka" [white lotus], a lotus qualified by whiteness is understood;
if this is so, and it is more appropriate to say that the meaning of a word is a positive injunction (vidhi), why then is apoha proclaimed? To this, [the reply is:]

It has been stated here that by the term "exclusion" (apoha), a positive entity (vidhi) qualified by the exclusion of others is expressed; in that case, while the positive entity is being cognized, there is a simultaneous cognition of the exclusion of others as its qualifier.
However, it is not appropriate to establish that perception (pratyakṣa) likewise has exclusion as its object.

Since there is no dispute regarding the fact that this verbal cognition has a real entity as its object— just like [the cognition of] a word— the term "affirmation" (vidhi) refers, according to conceptual determination (adhyavasāya), to an external object excluded from what is not that form;
and according to appearance (pratibhāsa), it refers to the form of the cognition itself.
In that regard, the external object is established as the denotation of a word solely through conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*);

it is not [established] through the vivid manifestation of its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), as is the case with perception, because there is no manifestation of a clearly evident specific characteristic restricted by place, time, and state. As the treatise states:

For even if there were a difference in the means, such as the eye and the word, the object would still appear in its own form. It has been said here as well:
"The basis for each mental state is indeed distinct from that of another;
how then can a single object possess a form that appears in diverse aspects?"
For two forms, one clear and one unclear, which are mutually contradictory, cannot belong to a single entity;
because if one were to appear in sensory cognition and the other in conceptual construction,
it would follow that the entity itself is divided.
For there is no distinction of entity other than a distinction of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*),
nor is there a distinction of intrinsic nature other than a distinction of appearance (*pratibhāsa*);
otherwise, the three worlds would constitute a single entity.

If it is argued that, although there is a difference between clear and indistinct appearances in a single tree for two persons situated at distant and near locations, there is no difference in the tree itself—[we reply:
we do not say that a difference in appearance is necessarily restricted to different objects; rather, we say it is necessarily restricted to the absence of having a single object.
Therefore, wherever there is a difference in appearance accompanied by a difference in causal efficiency and so forth, there is a difference in the real entity, as in the case of a jar.
On the other hand, in another case, since it does not abandon its status as having a single object due to a fixed rule, the single appearance is erroneous.
By this, that which Vācaspati said [is refuted]:

Nor is it the case that there is no difference in cognition between verbal and perceptual cognitions when they have real entities as their objects, because the distinction between mediacy and immediacy is established by the difference in their causes. That [argument] is not useful,
because it fails to prove that a mediate cognition has a real entity as its object.
However, the distinction of causes based on being beyond the senses is fulfilled simply by the absence of the apprehension of an object within the range of the sense organs.

Therefore, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not manifest in verbal cognition; furthermore, if a thing whose nature is a particular characteristic were the denotable object, then because it would be cognized in its entirety, affirmation and negation would be impossible.
For if it exists, the statement "it exists" is redundant,
and "it does not exist" is contradictory;
if it does not exist, "it does not exist" is redundant, and "it exists" is contradictory.
Furthermore, there is the employment of words such as "exists" (*asti*) and so forth.

Therefore, the fact that the appearance of a word is common to both the existence and non-existence of an external object does not justify its being the [direct] referent of that word. And as for what Vācaspati stated—having himself first introduced the theory that the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) are both denotable—he immediately thereafter said: "Nor is it untenable that the universal, which is the meaning of a word, is common to both existence and non-existence."

For although it is eternal by its own nature, because it resides in numerous individuals scattered across space and time, it becomes common to both existence and non-existence, and thus capable of being related to both "is" and "is not.

For the existence of a universal (*jāti*) consists in its connection with a present individual, while its non-existence consists in its connection with past and future individuals. Thus, it has been lamented that its commonality to existence and non-existence is either inconclusive due to a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekitva*), or else it is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*).
In that case, there is no injury to the present subject;
for by one who places the burden on the universal (jāti), the fact that the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is inexpressible is itself accepted.
Furthermore, in all cases, the existence and so forth of an object are considered solely in terms of its nature as a specific characteristic.
To claim that the relation of a universal (jāti) to a present individual and so forth constitutes its existence and other properties is a deception of the ignorant.
Likewise, there is a fault even in the view that a word denotes both the universal and the individual;
for if the cognition of the individual is established [by the word], [the universal is redundant].
Whether the universal (jāti) is understood as predominant or not,
there is no liberation from the defect regarding the cognition of the individual (vyakti).
This is not what is asserted by the followers of Kumārila:
that because a thing possesses a commonality (*sabhāgatva*), there is no fault of over-extension;
for it is the state of being a tree (*vṛkṣatva*)—undetermined as to whether it exists or does not exist—that is understood from the word.
That it is connected with one of those two as understood through another word is also inconsistent;
for when a permanent universal is apprehended, it is impossible for its existence or non-existence to remain undetermined.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the manner in which words convey their meaning here is not like that of perception— such that there would be no need for words like "exists" (asti) and so forth, just as in the case of what is seen [by perception]—

this too has been refuted by the critique of the "distinct appearance" (bhinnāvabhāsa) regarding the fact that sensory perception and verbal cognition grasp a single nature. Moreover, the diversity of the capacities of the means of knowledge (pramāṇas) is already accounted for by direct perception (sākṣātkāra) and conceptual determination (adhyavasāya).

Therefore, if the verbal expression were to present an object that is [already] perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then its manifestation would be exactly like that [perception]; and since it does not so manifest, it cannot be said to reveal that as its object.

If it is argued: "But surely, when the aspect of 'treeness' is indicated by the word 'tree,' the words 'is' (*asti*) and so forth are employed in order to ascertain the aspect of 'existence' (*sattva*) and the rest"?

Since the particular (svalakṣaṇa), which is apprehended by perception as being partless, has no room for another word, what opportunity is there for the affirmation or negation of other properties by means of another instrument of knowledge (pramāṇa)?
If it is argued that even in the case of perception, there is a dependence on another instrument of knowledge?
Let it be granted that [perception] lacks a determinate nature regarding an object whose specific form has not been previously cultivated;

however, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), being itself determinate by nature, requires nothing else for that which it grasps. Yet, since there is a dependence on words, other inferential signs (*liṅga*), and so forth, the grasping of the actual thing's own-form (*svarūpa*) does not occur.

Now, it may be argued that since properties such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth are distinct from one another and from the substratum (*dharmin*), even when the tree is cognized by way of a single property characterized by its genus, there is no cognition of it as possessing other properties; why then is the comprehension of other distinct properties— such as being blue, moving, or very tall— not dependent upon their separate denotation?
This is inconsistent;
for the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is an undivided whole, appears in perception.

Since the distinction between property (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*)—which is observable—is refuted by perception, otherwise there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that everything would exist everywhere.

It has been established in the treatise that the conventional usage of property (*dharma*) and its possessor (*dharmī*) is based on an imagined distinction; or, even if a real distinction between property and its possessor were to exist,
since their relation through inherence (*samavāya*) and so forth has been refuted, a proximity characterized by mutual assistance must be accepted.

And thus, just as in the case of perception, when a substratum (*dharmin*) is apprehended through the proximity of the sense organ, there is the apprehension of all its properties (*dharma*); so too, when a substratum is apprehended by means of a word or a logical mark (*liṅga*)— both of which are bound by relations such as that of the signified and the signifier— there would likewise be the apprehension of all its properties without exception,
since the mere fact of proximity is no different [in these cases].
And as Vācaspati [says]:
"When that [entity] qualified by one limiting adjunct (upādhi) has been apprehended as existent, there is no apprehension of it as qualified by another limiting adjunct."
For the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a substance is indeed qualified by adventitious attributes (*upādhi*);
however, neither the attributes nor the state of being qualified constitute its intrinsic nature.
Thus, that [position] also floats away [is untenable].
For it is not the case that the apprehension of another attribute (upādhi) follows from non-difference;
for only by presupposing difference can one entail the apprehension of the beneficiary (upakārya) upon the apprehension of the benefactor (upakāraka).
Nor is it appropriate to conceive of a restriction between a property and its locus based on their intrinsic nature alone, as is the case with the causal relation between fire and smoke.
For even those two are not established by valid means of cognition (pramāṇa);
and the rule is that the description of an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) applies only to that which is established by a valid means of cognition.

As for the objection raised here by Nyāyabhūṣaṇa—that the perception of the sun and other planets would entail the perception of the entire mass of objects assisted by them—that is merely the result of failing to grasp his intended meaning. For in your own view, there is a distinction between the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin), and the relation [between them] is defined solely as assistance (upakāra).
Therefore, when the assistant is perceived, it was argued that only the assisted object—which occupies the same location and exists in the form of a property—would be perceived.

How, then, is it logical that there could be the consequence of perceiving another substance— which is a distinct object located in a different place and whose deviation [from the universal] has been observed— by means of the sun? Therefore, since the nature of the thing is apprehended through even a single property, and thus its entire essence is cognized,
what room is there for affirmation or negation by means of another word?
And since it does exist, it is established that the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is not what appears to words, conceptual constructions, or logical marks.

Nor is the universal that which appears in verbal cognition; for when one hears the word "cows" from the expression "cows are grazing on the far bank of the river," there appear [in the mind] forms such as dewlaps, horns, and tails, surrounded by the shapes of syllables, appearing as if condensed because of the non-consideration of differences among members of the same class—
and yet, that very thing is not the universal.

Indeed, the state of being a limb is said to be empty of color, shape, syllables, and form; and that very same thing, consisting merely of a dewlap, horns, and so forth— which, although entirely distinct from every individual instance— is unified with the particular (svalakṣaṇa) and thus called a "universal" (sāmānya)—
is nothing but an error, because such an external object is not actually attained, just like the appearance of [illusory] hair.
Therefore, let this be an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of cognition itself in that form due to the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); or let that form appear as something non-existent;
or let the individuals themselves appear otherwise by disregarding their mutual differences, because of the intervention of memory.
Or let it be called a lapse of memory;
in any case, this cognition of a universal is indeed devoid of an object— where is there even talk of a universal?
Furthermore, as for the claim that the cognition of a universal would be causeless in the absence of a real universal, that is incorrect.

For it is the causal complex—augmented by the perception of a previous individual and a staff, and by memory—which, producing a cognition of a non-distinct [object], generates a conceptual construction of a universal that lacks an external object.
Thus, in verbal cognition, a genus does not appear.
Nor is there establishment [of this] through perception, nor even through inference;
for, since it is invisible, no connected logical mark (liṅga) is observed.
Nor is its establishment like that of the sense faculties.
Because an occasional effect of cognition establishes the existence of some other efficient cause [distinct from the object];
even when one might point out the absence of the cognition "cow" within another individual body or in the interval between them,

since all individual cow-bodies such as the *śābaleya* and others would then be absent, the resulting absence of the cognition "cow" would be logically accounted for— how could it imply a separate entity [such as a universal]?
The cow-individual exists precisely because of "cowness";
otherwise, even a horse would be a cow-individual.
If it were so, "cowness" would exist precisely because of the cow-individual; otherwise, even horseness would be cowness.
Therefore, it is precisely from this causal succession that the cow-individual [arises], whether or not "cowness" exists as a separate entity.

Now, if the capacity to produce the cognition of a universal were non-different from a single individual, then another individual excluded from those of a different class would be incapable [of producing that cognition].
If it is argued that when [the capacity] is distinct, then that very thing is the universal, and there is merely a dispute over the name—[we reply:
that power is indeed non-distinct with respect to each object.
Just as one entity possesses a nature capable [of producing an effect], so too does another; what kind of fault does this entail?

Just as for you, even a single universal (*jāti*) is the cause for producing a common verbal expression, and another [universal] is likewise [the cause] by its own nature alone, independent of other universals;
so too for us, the individual (*vyakti*) is also independent of universals and is the cause [of differentiation] by its own nature alone.
As for what Trilocana [says]:
The inherence of universals and particulars, such as "horseness" and "cowness," in their own substrata is the universal;
it is the cause of the designation and cognition "universal.
If this is so, then let this very same thing be the cause of such designation and cognition even with respect to individuals.
Why accept a universal through such negligence? Nor is inherence possible.
The cognition "it is here" establishes inherence, and the cognition "it is here" would occur only upon seeing two things;
yet, since there is no dependence on such an object anywhere, this [inherence] is merely one's own conceptual construction and thus a mere expedient.

By this, his objection— namely, "How can this recurrence of a cognition, which follows a recurring entity, be possible in the case of individuals that are absolutely distinct and whose cognitions follow only excluded (particular) objects?"—
is refuted; for there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of universals themselves, which, though mutually excluded, are perceived as recurring through a recurring cognition.

Furthermore, as for the subverting argument he has stated regarding the contrary case— namely, that "the persistence of verbal expression and cognition, occurring only in certain instances after having ceased elsewhere,
must have a cause; and there is no other cause," and so forth— [this is addressed as follows].
That is not correct;

for it has already been established that the persistence of denotation and cognition occurs even without a persisting [universal], because one must necessarily accept a specific nature that is excluded from what is not that [nature].
Therefore, by whatever proximity a universal extends over things that are equally distinct—
"Let that very [proximity] which exists in one case and not elsewhere be the basis for the verbal cognition; why [posit a separate relation]?

Furthermore, as for what was stated here by the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*: "It is not the case that the very same proximity by which a staff, a thread, and so forth extend in one place and not elsewhere, should be the basis for the conventional usage of 'one possessing a staff' (*daṇḍin*) or 'possessing a thread' (*sūtrin*) in the cases of a person, a crystal, and so on. Why [is this said]?"
The argument beginning with "by means of the staff, the thread, and so forth" is inconsistent;

for when a staff and a thread are seen in close proximity to a person and a crystal respectively, their status as causes for the cognition of "one with a staff" (daṇḍin) and "one with a thread" (sūtrin) is not denied.
A universal, however, is not observed even in a dream;
therefore, if this [universal] must be postulated, it would be better to postulate that proximity itself is the cause of the cognition of a universal—
since there is no understanding of the intention behind why one should resort to such a cumbersome postulation.
Now, this inference establishing [the existence of] birth (jāti) is stated:
whatever is a qualified cognition is necessarily preceded by the apprehension of its qualifier,
just as the cognition of a man with a staff.
This specific cognition, "this is a cow," is by implication an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).
For in the example, the specific cognition is established as the effect of the experience of the qualifier. To this, the following objection is raised:
Alternatively, what is to be proven is either that a specific cognition is necessarily preceded by the apprehension of distinct qualifiers,
or that it is necessarily preceded by the experience of the qualifiers alone.
In the first case, the thesis is contradicted by perception, which leaves no room for the application of the proof.
Because perception, which grasps a real entity, lacks the appearance of both [the particular and the universal],
and because being a qualified cognition is [itself] a universal,
the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Because it is observed even without the apprehension of distinct qualifiers,
as in the cases: "the pot possesses its own nature" or "cowness is a universal."

In the second case, however, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). This is because, just as in the case of "the pot possesses its own nature" (*svarūpavān ghaṭaḥ*), the relation of qualifier and qualified is accepted by resorting to a conceptualized distinction, such as "the individual possesses the universal cowness" (*gotvajātimān piṇḍaḥ*); for the linguistic usage "this is a cow" is produced by an experience that excludes non-cows.

That very [perception] is not a cognition of a universal; and there exists a subverting cognition in the form of a sharp direct perception that apprehends only the individual, which serves as a refutation of the entire cycle of limiting adjuncts such as universals, qualities, and actions.
Or rather, the non-perception of the perceptible is well-established.
Thus, in this way, the word-meaning is indeed a positive entity (vidhi);
and that is intended to be either an external object or a mental form (buddhyākāra).
In that regard, there is neither affirmation nor negation of the form of cognition, either in reality or conventionally,
because it is accessible through the direct perception of self-awareness and because it is not subject to conceptual determination.
Nor do affirmation and negation apply to the external object in reality, because it does not appear in verbal cognition.

For this very reason, all phenomena are inexpressible in reality, due to the absence of both appearance and conceptual determination. Therefore, affirmation and negation pertain only to the external object on the conventional level; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the collapse of worldly transactional practice. Thus it is.
In reality, there is no proof by means of a positive injunction for either the form or the external object;
for while it exists externally according to conventional truth, it does not exist even conventionally as a formal essence.
By this, [the case of] Yaḍvarmmottara is explained.
To claim that there is both affirmation and negation of an "externality" that has been superimposed—something that is neither worldly, nor scriptural, nor philosophical—is to speak nonsense;
that has already been refuted.
Now, if in a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) the object to be determined (*adhyavaseya*) does not appear, then what is the meaning of saying "that has been determined"?
If it is asked: "Even though there is no appearance [of the object], what is the meaning of saying that it has been made the object of engagement?
And since there is no distinction in the absence of appearance, how can engagement be restricted to a specific object to the exclusion of other objects?

It is said in reply: Although the entire universe is not apprehended, nevertheless, because conceptualization is produced by a restricted causal complex, it possesses a restricted form and a restricted capacity; therefore, engagement occurs only with respect to water and so forth.

Just as smoke generates the cognition of a fire that is beyond the senses, entities have restricted objects and their natures are determined by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); they do not admit of questioning regarding a confusion of their capacities.
Therefore, the determination of that [object] arises from its connection with a specific form, which constitutes the production of activity directed toward it.

Nor do we say that activity occurs through superimposition based on similarity, which would provide an opening for criticism regarding either the form [of the cognition] being superimposed upon the external object, or the external object being superimposed upon the form.

Rather, the cognition itself, arising by the power of the maturation of its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), although not perceiving the external, extends its activity toward the external; thus it is indeed erroneous (*vipluta*).
Thus, it is established that the positive entity (*vidhi*) is an object qualified by the absence of others and excluded from those of a different class;
this very thing is what is denoted by the term "exclusion" (*apoha*), and it is the meaning of words as well as the objective domain for engagement and withdrawal.
Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*):
Whatever is expressive has as its object only the thing-in-itself (*vastumātra*) as determined by the exclusion of what does not possess that form (*atadrūpaparāvṛtta*).
For example, the statement "there is water in this well."
This form of words such as "cow" and so forth is a denoter; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
It is not unestablished (*asiddha*), even though, according to the reasoning previously stated, there is an absence of an ultimately real relationship between the denoted and the denoter.
Because that which is produced by conceptual determination must necessarily be accepted by all those engaged in worldly transaction;
otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the cessation of all worldly activity.
Nor is it contradictory, because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
Nor is [the reason] inconclusive;

for those opponents who do not accept that words have as their object merely the thing-in-itself (vastumātra) as determined by the exclusion of heterogeneous things (vijātivyāvṛtta), must [admit that] the ultimate referent (paramārthataḥ) is either the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), or an attribute (upādhi), or the connection with an attribute (upādhiyoga).
Let it be that the intellect possesses an adjunct (sopādhi), or let it possess an action (kṛti), because there is no other alternative;
for if it were not an object, it would be impossible for it to be expressive. In that case:

There is no [independent] convention at the beginning or the end because of the loss of the power of the fruit; nor is it appropriate in the middle, due to the absence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) in all three ways.

Thus, since there is no other denotable object, when the pervader characterized by having an object is excluded, expressiveness—which is excluded from the counter-example—is pervaded by the state of having a determined external object; this is the establishment of the pervasion.
First, the primary meaning is expressed by words, while exclusion (apoha) is understood therein as a subordinate quality.
The referent is one from the perspective of superimposition, another from the perspective of appearance, or it may be established as something else; but in reality, there is no referent at all.
The Proof of Apoha is completed.
This is the work of the great scholar Ratnakīrti.
Let there be this proliferation for the clever in the process of exclusion (apoha); however, the failure to manifest the actual nature of the thing is the vital point.
If that [nature] is not firmly established, everything collapses without effort; but if it is firmly established, then well-being follows by that much alone.
This refutation of Kīrtti was easily composed by Trailokyadatta over the course of two watches of the night; therefore, for the sake of himself and others, it must be preserved with effort.
